text:
The ratio of mass percentage (w/w) of C : H in a hydrocarbon is 12 : 1.  It has two carbon atoms. The weight (in g) of $CO_{2}(g)$ formed when 3.38 g of this hydrocarbon is completely burnt in oxygen is : 

(Given : Molar mass in g mol$^{–1} C$ : 12, H : 1, O : 16)
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 2nd April Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
Let the hydrocarbon be $C_{2}H_{x}$ since it has two carbon atoms.

Given, the mass percentage ratio of $C:H$ is $12:1$.

So, in the hydrocarbon,

mass of carbon $=2\times 12=24$

mass of hydrogen $=x\times 1=x$

Now,

$24:x=12:1$

So,

$\frac{24}{x}=\frac{12}{1}$

$24=12x$

$x=2$

Hence, the hydrocarbon is

$C_{2}H_{2}$

Its molar mass is

$(2\times 12)+(2\times 1)=24+2=26\text{g mol}^{-1}$

Number of moles of $C_{2}H_{2}$ in $3.38$ g:

$\text{moles of}C_{2}H_{2}=\frac{3.38}{26}=0.13\text{mol}$

Complete combustion of acetylene:

$2C_{2}H_{2}+5O_{2}\to 4CO_{2}+2H_{2}O$

From the equation,

$1\text{mol}C_{2}H_{2}\to 2\text{mol}CO_{2}$

Therefore,

$0.13\text{mol}C_{2}H_{2}\to 0.26\text{mol}CO_{2}$

Molar mass of $CO_{2}$:

$12+(2\times 16)=44\text{g mol}^{-1}$

Mass of $CO_{2}$ formed:

$0.26\times 44=11.44\text{g}$

So, the correct answer is

$11.44\text{g}$

Option B.

text: The first and second ionization constants of a weak dibasic acid $H_{2}A$ are $8.1\times 10^{-8}$ and $1.0\times 10^{-13}$ respectively. 0.1 mol of $H_{2}A$ was dissolved in 1 L of 0.1 M HCl solution. The concentration of $HA^{-}$ in the resultant solution is:
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 2nd April Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
Given:

First ionization constant:  

$K_{a1}=8.1\times 10^{-8}$

Second ionization constant:  

$K_{a2}=1.0\times 10^{-13}$

$0.1$ mol of $H_{2}A$ is dissolved in $1\text{L}$ of $0.1\text{M HCl}$

So, in the final solution:

Initial concentration of $H_{2}A=0.1\text{M}$

Since HCl is a strong acid,  

$[H^{+}]=0.1\text{M}$

We have to find $[HA^{-}]$.

For the first dissociation of dibasic acid:

$H_{2}A⇌H^{+}+HA^{-}$

Using the expression of first ionization constant,

$K_{a1}=\frac{[H^{+}][HA^{-}]}{[H_{2}A]}$

Substitute the known values:

$8.1\times 10^{-8}=\frac{(0.1)[HA^{-}]}{0.1}$

Since $\dfrac{0.1}{0.1}=1$, we get:

$[HA^{-}]=8.1\times 10^{-8}\text{M}$

Now, because $K_{a2}$ is extremely small, further dissociation of $HA^{-}$ is negligible in presence of strong acid.

Hence, the concentration of $HA^{-}$ in the resultant solution is

$8.1\times 10^{-8}\text{M}$

So, the correct option is:

$\text{Option C}$

text:
SF${}_{4}$ is isostructural with :
A. BrF${}_{4}^{⊖}$
B. CH${}_{4}$
C. IF${}_{4}^{⊕}$
D. XeF${}_{4}$
E. XeO${}_{2}$F${}_{2}$
Choose the correct answer from the options given below :
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 2nd April Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
$\mathrm{SF}{}_{4}$: S has 6 valence electrons, forming 4 bond pairs and keeping 1 lone pair, so 5 electron pairs ($\mathrm{sp}^{3}\mathrm{d}$) give a see-saw shape.

$\mathrm{BrF}{}_{4}{}^{-}$ (A): Br has $7+1=8$ electrons, giving 4 bond pairs and 2 lone pairs ($\mathrm{sp}^{3}\mathrm{d}^{2}$), so it is square planar.

$\mathrm{CH}{}_{4}$ (B): 4 bond pairs and no lone pair ($\mathrm{sp}^{3}$), so it is tetrahedral.

$\mathrm{IF}{}_{4}{}^{+}$ (C): I has $7-1=6$ electrons, giving 4 bond pairs and 1 lone pair ($\mathrm{sp}^{3}\mathrm{d}$), so it is see-saw.

$\mathrm{XeF}{}_{4}$ (D): 4 bond pairs and 2 lone pairs ($\mathrm{sp}^{3}\mathrm{d}^{2}$), so it is square planar.

$\mathrm{XeO}{}_{2}\mathrm{F}{}_{2}$ (E): Xe uses 6 of its 8 electrons in two Xe=O and two Xe–F bonds and keeps 1 lone pair, so 4 σ bond pairs and 1 lone pair ($\mathrm{sp}^{3}\mathrm{d}$) give a see-saw shape.

$\mathrm{SF}{}_{4}$ is isostructural with $\mathrm{IF}{}_{4}{}^{+}$ (C) and $\mathrm{XeO}{}_{2}\mathrm{F}{}_{2}$ (E).

Hence, the correct option is (B).

text: Gas 'A' undergoes change from state 'X' to state 'Y'. In this process, the heat absorbed and work done by the gas is 10 J and 18 J respectively. Now gas is brought back to state 'X' by another process during which 6 J of heat is evolved. In the reverse process of 'Y' to 'X',
options: 18 J of the work is done by the gas 'A'.
2 J of the work is done by the gas 'A'.
12 J of the work is done on the gas 'A' by the surrounding.
14 J of the work is done on the gas 'A' by the surrounding.
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 2nd April Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
In the chemistry (IUPAC) sign convention, $\Delta U=q+w$, where $q>0$ for heat absorbed by the gas and $w>0$ for work done on the gas.

Process X $\to$ Y: heat absorbed $q=+10\text{J}$; 18 J of work is done by the gas, so $w=-18\text{J}$.

$\Delta U_{X\to Y}=10+(-18)=-8\text{J}$

Internal energy is a state function, so for the return from Y to X by any path, $\Delta U_{Y\to X}=+8\text{J}$.

Process Y $\to$ X: 6 J of heat is evolved, so $q=-6\text{J}$.

$8=-6+w\Rightarrow w=+14\text{J}$

A positive $w$ means 14 J of work is done on gas A by the surroundings.

Hence, the correct option is (D).
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2026 (Online) 2nd April Evening Shift

text:
Solution A is prepared by dissolving 1 g of a protein (molar mass = 50,000 g mol$^{-1})$ in 0.5 L of water at 300 K. Its osmotic pressure is $x$ bar. Solution B is made by dissolving 2 g of the same protein in 1 L of water at 300 K. Osmotic pressure of solution B is $y$ bar. Entire solution of A is mixed with entire solution of B at the same temperature. The osmotic pressure of resultant solution is $z$ bar. $x$, $y$ and $z$ respectively are:
(R = 0.083 L bar mol$^{-1} K^{-1})$
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 2nd April Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
For osmotic pressure, we use the NCERT relation:

$π=CRT=\frac{n}{V}RT$

where

$π$ = osmotic pressure

$n$ = number of moles of solute

$V$ = volume of solution

$R=0.083\text{L bar mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$

$T=300\text{K}$

Protein molar mass is:

$M=50000\text{g mol}^{-1}$

Now solve each part.

For solution A
Mass of protein $=1\text{g}$

Moles of protein:

$n_{A}=\frac{1}{50000}=2\times 10^{-5}\text{mol}$

Volume:

$V_{A}=0.5\text{L}$

So concentration:

$C_{A}=\frac{2\times 10^{-5}}{0.5}=4\times 10^{-5}\text{mol L}^{-1}$

Hence osmotic pressure:

$x=π_{A}=C_{A}RT$

$x=(4\times 10^{-5})(0.083)(300)$

First calculate:

$0.083\times 300=24.9$

So,

$x=4\times 10^{-5}\times 24.9=9.96\times 10^{-4}\text{bar}$

For solution B
Mass of protein $=2\text{g}$

Moles:

$n_{B}=\frac{2}{50000}=4\times 10^{-5}\text{mol}$

Volume:

$V_{B}=1\text{L}$

Concentration:

$C_{B}=\frac{4\times 10^{-5}}{1}=4\times 10^{-5}\text{mol L}^{-1}$

Thus,

$y=π_{B}=C_{B}RT$

$y=(4\times 10^{-5})(0.083)(300)$

$y=9.96\times 10^{-4}\text{bar}$

After mixing A and B
Total moles of protein:

$n_{\text{total}}=2\times 10^{-5}+4\times 10^{-5}=6\times 10^{-5}\text{mol}$

Total volume:

$V_{\text{total}}=0.5+1=1.5\text{L}$

Concentration after mixing:

$C_{\text{mix}}=\frac{6\times 10^{-5}}{1.5}=4\times 10^{-5}\text{mol L}^{-1}$

Again,

$z=π_{\text{mix}}=C_{\text{mix}}RT$

$z=(4\times 10^{-5})(0.083)(300)=9.96\times 10^{-4}\text{bar}$

So,

$x=9.96\times 10^{-4}\text{bar},y=9.96\times 10^{-4}\text{bar},z=9.96\times 10^{-4}\text{bar}$

Therefore, the correct option is:

$\text{Option A}$
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2026 (Online) 2nd April Evening Shift

text:
At 25°C, 20.0 mL of 0.2 M weak monoprotic acid HX is titrated against 0.2 M NaOH. The pH of the solution (a) at the start of the titration (when NaOH has not been added) and (b) when 10 mL of NaOH is added respectively, are :
Given :
$K_{a}=5\times 10^{-4}$
$\mathrm{p}K_{a}=3.3$
$α\ll 1$
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 2nd April Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
Given data:

Concentration of the weak acid $HX$, $C=0.2\text{M}$

Initial volume of $HX=20.0\text{mL}$

Concentration of $NaOH=0.2\text{M}$

Dissociation constant of acid, $K_{a}=5\times 10^{-4}$

$\mathrm{p}K_{a}=3.3$

Case (a): At the start of the titration (when NO $NaOH$ has been added)

At this point, only the weak acid $HX$ is present in the solution. Since the degree of dissociation $α\ll 1$, we can calculate the hydrogen ion concentration $[H^{+}]$ using the formula for a weak monoprotic acid:

$[H^{+}]=\sqrt{K_{a}\times C}$

Substitute the values of $K_{a}$ and $C$:

$[H^{+}]=\sqrt{5\times 10^{-4}\times 0.2}$

$[H^{+}]=\sqrt{1\times 10^{-4}}$

$[H^{+}]=10^{-2}\text{M}$

The $\text{pH}$ of the solution is:

$\text{pH}=-\log [H^{+}]$

$\text{pH}=-\log (10^{-2})=2.0$

Case (b): When $10\text{mL}$ of $0.2\text{M}NaOH$ is added

When strong base $NaOH$ is added, it reacts with the weak acid $HX$ to form salt $NaX$ and water:

$HX+NaOH⟶NaX+H_{2}O$

Let us find the number of millimoles (mmol) of acid and base:

$\text{Initial millimoles of}HX=\text{Molarity}\times \text{Volume in mL}=0.2\text{M}\times 20.0\text{mL}=4.0\text{mmol}$

$\text{Millimoles of}NaOH\text{added}=0.2\text{M}\times 10.0\text{mL}=2.0\text{mmol}$

Since $NaOH$ is the limiting reagent, $2.0\text{mmol}$ of $NaOH$ will completely neutralize $2.0\text{mmol}$ of $HX$, forming $2.0\text{mmol}$ of the salt $NaX$. 

Let's analyze the composition of the mixture after the reaction:

$\text{Remaining millimoles of}HX=4.0-2.0=2.0\text{mmol}$

$\text{Millimoles of salt}NaX\text{formed}=2.0\text{mmol}$

Now, the solution contains a weak acid ($HX$) and its salt with a strong base ($NaX$). This constitutes an acidic buffer solution. We can determine the $\text{pH}$ using the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation:

$\text{pH}=\mathrm{p}K_{a}+\log \left (\frac{[\text{Salt}]}{[\text{Acid}]}\right )$

Since the volumes are the same, the ratio of their concentrations is simply the ratio of their millimoles:

$\text{pH}=3.3+\log \left (\frac{2.0}{2.0}\right )$

$\text{pH}=3.3+\log (1)$

Since $\log (1)=0$:

$\text{pH}=3.3+0=3.3$ 

(Note: We can also directly observe that because exactly half the equivalence volume of the base is added, it is the half-neutralization point, where $\text{pH}=\mathrm{p}K_{a}$.)

Conclusion:

The $\text{pH}$ values for part (a) and (b) are $2.0$ and $3.3$ respectively. 

Correct Option: Option B
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2026 (Online) 2nd April Evening Shift

text:
Consider the reaction aX → bY, for which the rate constant at 30°C is $1\times 10^{-3}\text{mol}^{-1}\text{L}\text{s}^{-1}$. Which of the following statements are true?

A. When concentration of ‘X’ is increased to four times, the rate of reaction becomes 16 times.

B. The reaction is a second order reaction.

C. The half-life period is independent of the concentration of X.

D. Decomposition of N${}_{2}$O${}_{5}$ is an example of the above reaction.

E. 
[IMG]
 vs time is valid for the above reaction.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
options: A, B, D and E Only
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 2nd April Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
The given rate constant is $k=10^{-3}\text{M}^{-1}\text{s}^{-1}$.

Step 1: Determining the order of reaction

The general unit of the rate constant is $\text{M}^{1-n}\qquad \text{s}^{-1}$, where $n$ is the order of reaction.  

Here, the unit of $k$ is $\text{M}^{-1}\text{s}^{-1}$.

So, $1-n=-1\Rightarrow n=2$.  

Hence, this is a second order reaction.

Step 2: Expression for the rate

The rate law for a second order reaction is:  

$\text{Rate}=k[A]^{2}$

Step 3: Effect of changing concentration

If the concentration of $A$ is made 4 times, that is, $[A]^{'}=4[A]$, then  

$\text{New rate}=k(4[A])^{2}=16k[A]^{2}$  

So, the rate increases by 16 times.  

Therefore, statement (A) is correct.

Step 4: Order of reaction

As we found $n=2$, the reaction is second order.  

So, statement (B) is correct.

Step 5: Half-life relation

For a second order reaction, the half-life is inversely proportional to the initial concentration:  

$t_{1/2}=\frac{1}{k[A]_{0}}$  

Hence, the half-life depends on concentration.  

So, statement (C) is incorrect because it is true only for a first order reaction.

Step 6: Example of reaction

The decomposition of $\mathrm{N}_{2}\mathrm{O}_{5}$ is a first order reaction.  

Thus, statement (D) is incorrect.

Step 7: Graph type

A straight-line graph of $\log \frac{[R]_{0}}{[R]_{t}}$ versus $t$ is valid only for first order reactions, not second order.  

Therefore, statement (E) is incorrect.

Final Answer: The correct statements are (A) and (B).
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2026 (Online) 2nd April Evening Shift

text: The correct set that contains all kinds (basic, acidic, amphoteric and neutral) of oxides is :
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 2nd April Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
To find the correct set, we need one oxide of each type:

Basic oxide

Acidic oxide

Amphoteric oxide

Neutral oxide

Now let us check the given oxides.

Important classifications

Basic oxides: Usually metallic oxides like $Na_{2}O$, $K_{2}O$

Acidic oxides: Usually non-metallic oxides like $Cl_{2}O_{7}$

Amphoteric oxides: Oxides that react with both acids and bases, like $Al_{2}O_{3}$, $As_{2}O_{3}$

Neutral oxides: Neither acidic nor basic, like $CO$, $NO$, $N_{2}O$

Option A
$Na_{2}O,K_{2}O,Al_{2}O_{3},As_{2}O_{3}$

$Na_{2}O$ = basic

$K_{2}O$ = basic

$Al_{2}O_{3}$ = amphoteric

$As_{2}O_{3}$ = amphoteric

This set does not contain acidic and neutral oxides.

So, Option A is incorrect.

Option B
$Al_{2}O_{3},As_{2}O_{3},CO,NO$

$Al_{2}O_{3}$ = amphoteric

$As_{2}O_{3}$ = amphoteric

$CO$ = neutral

$NO$ = neutral

This set does not contain basic and acidic oxides.

So, Option B is incorrect.

Option C
$K_{2}O,Cl_{2}O_{7},As_{2}O_{3},NO$

$K_{2}O$ = basic

$Cl_{2}O_{7}$ = acidic

$As_{2}O_{3}$ = amphoteric

$NO$ = neutral

This set contains all four kinds of oxides.

So, Option C is correct.

Option D
$Na_{2}O,N_{2}O,Al_{2}O_{3},CO$

$Na_{2}O$ = basic

$N_{2}O$ = neutral

$Al_{2}O_{3}$ = amphoteric

$CO$ = neutral

This set does not contain any acidic oxide.

So, Option D is incorrect.

Final Answer
$\text{Option C}$

text:
Given below are two statements :
Statement I: The second ionization enthalpy of B, Al and Ga is in the order of B > Al > Ga.
Statement II: The correct order in terms of first ionization enthalpy is Si correct answer from the options given below :
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 2nd April Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
For boron family elements, the order of second ionization enthalpy is:

$\mathrm{B}_{(2427\mathrm{KJ}/\mathrm{mol})}>\mathrm{Ga}_{(1979\mathrm{KJ}/\mathrm{mol})}>\mathrm{Al}_{(1816\mathrm{KJ}/\mathrm{mol})}$

So, the given order $\mathrm{B}>\mathrm{Al}>\mathrm{Ga}$ is incorrect.

For carbon family elements, the order of first ionization enthalpy is:

$\mathrm{Si}_{(786\mathrm{KJ}/\mathrm{mol})}>\mathrm{Ge}_{(761\mathrm{KJ}/\mathrm{mol})}>\mathrm{Pb}_{(715\mathrm{KJ}/\mathrm{mol})}>\mathrm{Sn}_{(708\mathrm{KJ}/\mathrm{mol})}$

So, the given order $\mathrm{Si}<\mathrm{Ge}<\mathrm{Pb}<\mathrm{Sn}$ is also incorrect.

Hence, both Statement I and Statement II are false.

text:
Given below are two statements :
 Statement I : Among Zn, Mn, Sc and Cu, the energy required to remove the third valence electron is highest for Zn and lowest for Sc.
 Statement II : The correct order of the following complexes in terms of CFSE is $[\text{Co(H}_{2}\text{O})_{6}]^{2+}<[\text{Co(H}_{2}\text{O})_{6}]^{3+}<[\text{Co(en)}_{3}]^{3+}$.
 In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below :
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 2nd April Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
Statement I
We need to compare the energy required to remove the third valence electron, that is, the third ionization enthalpy.

First write the electronic configurations:

$Zn:[Ar]3d^{10}4s^{2}$

$Mn:[Ar]3d^{5}4s^{2}$

$Sc:[Ar]3d^{1}4s^{2}$

$Cu:[Ar]3d^{10}4s^{1}$

Now, after removal of two electrons:

$Zn^{2+}:[Ar]3d^{10}$

$Mn^{2+}:[Ar]3d^{5}$

$Sc^{2+}:[Ar]3d^{1}$

$Cu^{2+}:[Ar]3d^{9}$

The third electron is now removed from these ions.

Which one will have highest third ionization enthalpy?
For $Zn^{2+}$, the configuration is $3d^{10}$, which is a completely filled and very stable configuration. Removing one electron from this is difficult.

So, third ionization enthalpy is highest for Zn.

Which one will have lowest third ionization enthalpy?
For $Sc^{2+}$, configuration is $3d^{1}$. Removing this one electron gives $Sc^{3+}:[Ar]$, which is a noble gas configuration, hence this removal is comparatively easier.

So, third ionization enthalpy is lowest for Sc.

Therefore, Statement I is true.

Statement II
We need the order of complexes in terms of CFSE.

Given complexes:

$[\text{Co(H}_{2}\text{O})_{6}]^{2+}$

$[\text{Co(H}_{2}\text{O})_{6}]^{3+}$

$[\text{Co(en)}_{3}]^{3+}$

Step 1: Find oxidation state and $d$-configuration

In $[\text{Co(H}_{2}\text{O})_{6}]^{2+}$, cobalt is $Co^{2+}$  

$Co:[Ar]3d^{7}4s^{2}$  

$Co^{2+}:3d^{7}$

In $[\text{Co(H}_{2}\text{O})_{6}]^{3+}$, cobalt is $Co^{3+}$  

$Co^{3+}:3d^{6}$

In $[\text{Co(en)}_{3}]^{3+}$, cobalt is also $Co^{3+}$  

so it is also $3d^{6}$

Step 2: Nature of ligand and spin state

$H_{2}O$ is a weak field ligand

$en$ is a stronger field ligand than $H_{2}O$

So:

$[\text{Co(H}_{2}\text{O})_{6}]^{2+}$ is octahedral, weak field, $d^{7}$  

generally high spin

$[\text{Co(H}_{2}\text{O})_{6}]^{3+}$ is octahedral, $d^{6}$  

because of higher charge on $Co^{3+}$, splitting is larger; this complex is effectively low spin

$[\text{Co(en)}_{3}]^{3+}$ is octahedral, $d^{6}$, strong field  

definitely low spin

Step 3: Calculate CFSE
1. $[\text{Co(H}_{2}\text{O})_{6}]^{2+}$ : high-spin $d^{7}$
Configuration: $t_{2g}^{5}e_{g}^{2}$

$CFSE=5(-0.4\Delta _{o})+2(+0.6\Delta _{o})=-2.0\Delta _{o}+1.2\Delta _{o}=-0.8\Delta _{o}$

Magnitude of CFSE $=0.8\Delta _{o}$

2. $[\text{Co(H}_{2}\text{O})_{6}]^{3+}$ : low-spin $d^{6}$
Configuration: $t_{2g}^{6}e_{g}^{0}$

$CFSE=6(-0.4\Delta _{o})=-2.4\Delta _{o}$

Magnitude $=2.4\Delta _{o}$

3. $[\text{Co(en)}_{3}]^{3+}$ : low-spin $d^{6}$
Also $t_{2g}^{6}e_{g}^{0}$, so

$CFSE=-2.4\Delta _{o}$

But here $en$ is stronger field than $H_{2}O$, so $\Delta _{o}$ is larger.

Hence CFSE magnitude is greater for $[\text{Co(en)}_{3}]^{3+}$ than for $[\text{Co(H}_{2}\text{O})_{6}]^{3+}$.

So the order is:

$[\text{Co(H}_{2}\text{O})_{6}]^{2+}<[\text{Co(H}_{2}\text{O})_{6}]^{3+}<[\text{Co(en)}_{3}]^{3+}$

Therefore, Statement II is also true.

Final Answer
$\text{Option A: Both Statement I and Statement II are true}$
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2026 (Online) 2nd April Evening Shift

text:
Which of the following complexes will show coordination isomerism?
A. $[\mathrm{Ag}(\mathrm{NH}_{3})_{2}][\mathrm{Ag}(\mathrm{CN})_{2}]$
B. $[\mathrm{Co}(\mathrm{NH}_{3})_{6}][\mathrm{Cr}(\mathrm{CN})_{6}]$
C. $[\mathrm{Co}(\mathrm{NH}_{3})_{6}][\mathrm{Co}(\mathrm{CN})_{6}]$
D. $[\mathrm{Fe}(\mathrm{NH}_{3})_{6}][\mathrm{Co}(\mathrm{CN})_{6}]$
E. $[\mathrm{Co}(\mathrm{NH}_{3})_{6}][\mathrm{Fe}(\mathrm{CN})_{6}]$
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 2nd April Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
Coordination Isomerism arises from the interchange of ligands between cationic and anionic entities of different metal ions present in a complex. When the complete interchange of ligands takes place, it must result in a new, chemically distinct isomer.

Let us evaluate each of the given choices under this concept:

A. $[\mathrm{Ag}(\mathrm{NH}_{3})_{2}][\mathrm{Ag}(\mathrm{CN})_{2}]$: Both the cationic and anionic entities contain the same metal ion ($\text{Ag}$). If we fully interchange the ligands, we get $[\mathrm{Ag}(\mathrm{CN})_{2}]^{-}[\mathrm{Ag}(\mathrm{NH}_{3})_{2}]^{+}$, which is exactly the same compound written in reverse order. Further, a partial interchange leads to neutral molecules $[\mathrm{Ag}(\mathrm{NH}_{3})(\mathrm{CN})]$, which destroys the cation-anion pair. Hence, it does not show coordination isomerism.

B. $[\mathrm{Co}(\mathrm{NH}_{3})_{6}][\mathrm{Cr}(\mathrm{CN})_{6}]$: This complex contains two different metal ions ($\text{Co}$ and $\text{Cr}$). By interchanging the ligands between the cationic and anionic coordination spheres, we get a completely new distinct complex: $[\mathrm{Cr}(\mathrm{NH}_{3})_{6}][\mathrm{Co}(\mathrm{CN})_{6}]$. Hence, it shows coordination isomerism. (This is also the classic example mentioned in NCERT).

C. $[\mathrm{Co}(\mathrm{NH}_{3})_{6}][\mathrm{Co}(\mathrm{CN})_{6}]$: Both entities contain the same metal ion ($\text{Co}$). A complete interchange of all ligands gives $[\mathrm{Co}(\mathrm{CN})_{6}]^{3-}[\mathrm{Co}(\mathrm{NH}_{3})_{6}]^{3+}$, which is exactly the same coordination compound. According to the strict NCERT definition requiring different metal ions for complete interchange, it does not exhibit coordination isomerism.

D. $[\mathrm{Fe}(\mathrm{NH}_{3})_{6}][\mathrm{Co}(\mathrm{CN})_{6}]$: This complex has two different metal ions ($\text{Fe}$ and $\text{Co}$). Exchanging the primary coordination spheres yields a distinct coordination isomer: $[\mathrm{Co}(\mathrm{NH}_{3})_{6}][\mathrm{Fe}(\mathrm{CN})_{6}]$. Hence, it shows coordination isomerism.

E. $[\mathrm{Co}(\mathrm{NH}_{3})_{6}][\mathrm{Fe}(\mathrm{CN})_{6}]$: This complex is exactly the coordination isomer of the complex described in option D. Since it consists of different metal ions ($\text{Co}$ and $\text{Fe}$), exchanging its ligands will yield the complex in D. Thus, it also shows coordination isomerism.

Conclusion:

Complexes B, D, and E exhibit coordination isomerism because they possess differently named metal ions in their cationic and anionic parts, allowing the exchange of ligands to produce distinctly new isomers. 

Correct Answer:

Option B (B, D and E Only)

text:
Complete combustion of $X$ g of an organic compound gave $0.25$ g of $CO_{2}$ and $0.12$ g of $H_{2}O$. If the % of carbon is $25%$ and of hydrogen is $4.89%$, then $X=–\times 10^{-3}$ g. (Nearest integer)

 (Molar mass of C, H and O are 12, 1 and 16 g mol${}^{-1}$ respectively.)
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 2nd April Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
For complete combustion, all the carbon in the compound goes into $CO_{2}$ and all the hydrogen goes into $H_{2}O$.

So first, let us find the masses of carbon and hydrogen present in the given sample.

1. Mass of carbon from $0.25$ g of $CO_{2}$
In $44$ g of $CO_{2}$, mass of carbon is $12$ g.

So, in $0.25$ g of $CO_{2}$, mass of carbon is

$\text{Mass of C}=\frac{12}{44}\times 0.25$

$=\frac{3}{44}=0.06818\text{g}$

2. Mass of hydrogen from $0.12$ g of $H_{2}O$
In $18$ g of $H_{2}O$, mass of hydrogen is $2$ g.

So, in $0.12$ g of $H_{2}O$, mass of hydrogen is

$\text{Mass of H}=\frac{2}{18}\times 0.12$

$=\frac{0.24}{18}=0.01333\text{g}$

3. Use given percentage of carbon
The compound contains $25%$ carbon.

If total mass of compound is $X$ g, then mass of carbon in it is

$\frac{25}{100}X=0.25X$

But this is equal to the carbon obtained from combustion:

$0.25X=0.06818$

So,

$X=\frac{0.06818}{0.25}=0.27272\text{g}$

$X\approx 0.273\text{g}$

Now write it in the form

$X=–\times 10^{-3}\text{g}$

Since

$0.273\text{g}=273\times 10^{-3}\text{g}$

So the required integer is

$273$

Therefore, the correct option is A.
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2026 (Online) 2nd April Evening Shift

Given below are two statements :
 Statement I : In 
[IMG]
, the carbocation is stabilised by +R effect of –OCH$_{3}$ group.
 Statement II : In

 In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below :
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 2nd April Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
Carbocation ($C^{+}$) has a deficiency of electrons, so it becomes more stable when a group donates electron density towards it.

Therefore, carbocations are stabilised by electron donating groups (EDGs) due to $+R,+I,+H$ effect whereas, carbanions ($C^{-}$) are stabilised by electron withdrawing groups (EWGs) due to $-R,-I,-H$ effect.
[IMG]


So, in Statement I, the $-OCH_{3}$ group shows $+R$ effect (lone pair donation), which stabilises the carbocation by resonance.


[IMG]


In Statement II, the $-NO_{2}$ group shows $-R$ effect (it withdraws electron density), which stabilises the carbanion by resonance.

text:
The compound (X) on
(i) on heating in the presence of anhydrous AlCl$_{3}$ and HCl gas gives 2,4-dimethyl pentane
(ii) aromatization gives toluene and
(iii) cyclisation gives methyl cyclohexane
The correct name of compound (X) is:
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 2nd April Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
All three changes are reactions of the alkane n-heptane, $\mathrm{C}{}_{7}\mathrm{H}{}_{16}$.

Heating n-heptane with anhydrous $\mathrm{AlCl}{}_{3}$ and $\mathrm{HCl}$ gas isomerises it to branched alkanes of the same formula, such as 2,4-dimethylpentane, $(\mathrm{CH}{}_{3}){}_{2}\mathrm{CHCH}{}_{2}\mathrm{CH}(\mathrm{CH}{}_{3}){}_{2}$.

Aromatisation over $\mathrm{Cr}{}_{2}\mathrm{O}{}_{3}$ at 773 K and 10–20 atm cyclises and dehydrogenates the chain to toluene:

$\mathrm{C}{}_{7}\mathrm{H}{}_{16}\longrightarrow \mathrm{C}{}_{6}\mathrm{H}{}_{5}\mathrm{CH}{}_{3}+4\mathrm{H}{}_{2}$


[IMG]

Cyclisation of the seven-carbon chain gives methylcyclohexane:

$\mathrm{C}{}_{7}\mathrm{H}{}_{16}\longrightarrow \mathrm{C}{}_{6}\mathrm{H}{}_{11}\mathrm{CH}{}_{3}+\mathrm{H}{}_{2}$

Hept-2-ene ($\mathrm{C}{}_{7}\mathrm{H}{}_{14}$) and the heptatrienes ($\mathrm{C}{}_{7}\mathrm{H}{}_{10}$) cannot give the saturated $\mathrm{C}{}_{7}\mathrm{H}{}_{16}$ on $\mathrm{AlCl}{}_{3}$/$\mathrm{HCl}$ isomerisation, since no hydrogen is added.

Hence, the correct option is (C).

text:
Correct statements regarding alkyl halides (R–X) among the following are :
 A. Alcohol being less polar solvent as compared to water, alcoholic KOH favours elimination reaction with R–X.
 B. Order of reactivity towards $S_{N}1$ mechanism is $C_{6}H_{5}–CH_{2}–Cl > C_{6}H_{5}–$CHCl$–C_{6}H_{5}$.
 C. Non substituted aryl halides exhibit properties similar to alkyl halides.
 D. Vinyl chloride is an example of haloalkene and allyl chloride is an example of haloalkyne.
 E. R–Cl can be prepared by reacting R–OH with SOCl$_{2}$ but Ar–Cl cannot be prepared by reacting Ar–OH with SOCl$_{2}$.
 Choose the correct answer from the options given below :
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 2nd April Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
Check each statement carefully.

For $R-X$, alcoholic KOH generally gives elimination, while aqueous KOH gives substitution.  

This happens because alcohol is less polar than water, so the hydroxide ion is less solvated and behaves more like a base, favouring $β$-elimination.

So, $A$ is correct.

Now $B$:

In $S_{N}1$ reaction, reactivity depends on stability of the carbocation formed.

For benzyl chloride:

$C_{6}H_{5}-CH_{2}-Cl\to C_{6}H_{5}-CH_{2}^{+}$

This is a benzyl carbocation, stabilized by resonance.

For benzhydryl chloride:

$C_{6}H_{5}-CHCl-C_{6}H_{5}\to C_{6}H_{5}-CH^{+}-C_{6}H_{5}$

This carbocation is stabilized by resonance with two phenyl rings, so it is more stable than benzyl carbocation.

Hence reactivity order should be

$C_{6}H_{5}-CHCl-C_{6}H_{5}>C_{6}H_{5}-CH_{2}-Cl$

So statement $B$ is false.

Now $C$:

Aryl halides do not show properties similar to alkyl halides.  

They are much less reactive in nucleophilic substitution because the $C-X$ bond in aryl halides has partial double bond character due to resonance.

So $C$ is false.

Now $D$:

Vinyl chloride, $CH_{2}=CHCl$, is a haloalkene. This part is correct.

Allyl chloride, $CH_{2}=CH-CH_{2}Cl$, is also a haloalkene, not a haloalkyne.

So $D$ is false.

Now $E$:

Alkyl chlorides can be prepared from alcohols using thionyl chloride:

$R-OH+SOCl_{2}\to R-Cl+SO_{2}+HCl$

But phenols do not give aryl chlorides with $SOCl_{2}$.  

In phenol, the $C-O$ bond has partial double bond character due to resonance, so replacement of $OH$ by $Cl$ does not happen this way.

So $E$ is correct.

The correct statements are $A$ and $E$ only.

$\text{Option C}$
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2026 (Online) 2nd April Evening Shift

text:
An organic compound “x” where molar ratio of C, O and H are equal, on treatment with 50% KOH under reflux followed by acidification produced “y”. The most likely structure of “y” is:
 [Molar mass of ‘x’ is 58 g mol$^{−1}$]
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 2nd April Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
The equal molar ratio of C, H and O gives the empirical formula $\mathrm{CHO}$, with empirical mass $29\text{g mol}^{-1}$. Since $M=58\text{g mol}^{-1}$, $n=2$ and x is $\mathrm{C}{}_{2}\mathrm{H}{}_{2}\mathrm{O}{}_{2}$, glyoxal, $\mathrm{OHC}-\mathrm{CHO}$.

Glyoxal has no $α$-hydrogen, so with 50% KOH it undergoes an intramolecular Cannizzaro reaction: one CHO group is oxidised to $\mathrm{COO}{}^{-}$ and the other is reduced to $\mathrm{CH}{}_{2}\mathrm{OH}$.

$\mathrm{OHC}-\mathrm{CHO}{}^{\mathrm{KOH}}\mathrm{HOCH}{}_{2}-\mathrm{COO}{}^{-}{}^{\mathrm{H}{}_{3}\mathrm{O}{}^{+}}\mathrm{HOCH}{}_{2}-\mathrm{COOH}$

So y is glycolic acid (2-hydroxyethanoic acid), $\mathrm{HOCH}{}_{2}\mathrm{COOH}$.

Hence, the correct option is (C).

text:
A molecule (X) with following structure under mild acidic condition is hydrolysed to produce (Y) and (Z). Identify the correct statements about (Y) and (Z).

[IMG]

A. Both (Y) and (Z) have same molar mass.
B. (Y) and (Z) can be distinguished from each other by NaHCO${}_{3}$.
C. (Y) and (Z) react with HCN with same rates.
D. (Y) and (Z) undergo addition reaction with 2,4-DNP.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below :
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 2nd April Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
X is $\mathrm{CH}{}_{3}-\mathrm{CH}=\mathrm{CH}-\mathrm{O}-\mathrm{C}(\mathrm{CH}{}_{3})=\mathrm{CH}{}_{2}$: the oxygen is bonded to two vinylic carbons, so both sides are enol ethers. Mild acid hydrolysis cleaves both C–O bonds and gives two enols, which tautomerise to carbonyl compounds.


[IMG]

The products are propanal, $\mathrm{CH}{}_{3}\mathrm{CH}{}_{2}\mathrm{CHO}$ (Y), and propanone, $\mathrm{CH}{}_{3}\mathrm{COCH}{}_{3}$ (Z).

Statement A is correct: both are $\mathrm{C}{}_{3}\mathrm{H}{}_{6}\mathrm{O}$, molar mass $58\text{g mol}^{-1}$.

Statement B is incorrect: neither compound has an acidic COOH group, so neither reacts with $\mathrm{NaHCO}{}_{3}$.

Statement C is incorrect: the aldehyde adds HCN faster than the ketone, because its carbonyl carbon is less hindered and more electrophilic.

Statement D is correct: both have a C=O group and react with 2,4-DNP (addition followed by loss of water) to give 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazones.

Hence, the correct option is (D).

text: Among $Fe^{2+}$, $Fe^{3+}$, $Cr^{2+}$ and $Zn^{2+}$, the ion that shows positive borax bead test and with highest ionisation enthalpy is :
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 2nd April Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
For a positive borax bead test, the ion must generally have unpaired electrons in its $d$-orbitals, because transition metal ions give characteristic bead colours due to electronic transitions.

Let us check each ion:

$Fe^{2+}:[Ar]3d^{6}$ → has unpaired electrons, so it gives borax bead test.

$Fe^{3+}:[Ar]3d^{5}$ → has unpaired electrons, so it gives borax bead test.

$Cr^{2+}:[Ar]3d^{4}$ → has unpaired electrons, so it gives borax bead test.

$Zn^{2+}:[Ar]3d^{10}$ → all electrons are paired, so it does not give a positive borax bead test.

So, among the given ions, we compare $Fe^{2+},Fe^{3+},Cr^{2+}$ for highest ionisation enthalpy.

Now, higher positive charge and greater effective nuclear charge generally mean higher ionisation enthalpy. Also, $Fe^{3+}$ has the stable half-filled configuration:

$Fe^{3+}=[Ar]3d^{5}$

This makes removal of another electron more difficult.

Therefore, the ion that:

shows positive borax bead test, and

has highest ionisation enthalpy

is

$Fe^{3+}$

So, the correct option is D. $Fe^{3+}$.
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2026 (Online) 2nd April Evening Shift

text:
The surface of sodium metal is irradiated with radiation of wavelength $x$ nm. The kinetic energy of ejected electrons is $2.8\times 10^{-20}\text{J}$. The work function of sodium is $2.3$ eV. The value of $x$ is $________$ $\times 10^{2}$ nm. (Nearest integer)
(Given: $h=6.6\times 10^{-34}\text{J s}$ ; $1\text{eV}=1.6\times 10^{-19}\text{J}$ ; $c=3.0\times 10^{8}\text{m s}^{-1}$)
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 2nd April Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
Using Einstein’s photoelectric equation,

$hν=𝜙+K_{\max }$

Also,

$hν=\frac{hc}{λ}$

So,

$\frac{hc}{λ}=𝜙+K_{\max }$

Now convert the work function into joule:

$𝜙=2.3\text{eV}=2.3\times 1.6\times 10^{-19}\text{J}$

$𝜙=3.68\times 10^{-19}\text{J}$

Given kinetic energy,

$K_{\max }=2.8\times 10^{-20}\text{J}$

Hence total photon energy is

$E=𝜙+K_{\max }$

$E=3.68\times 10^{-19}+2.8\times 10^{-20}$

$E=3.96\times 10^{-19}\text{J}$

Now,

$λ=\frac{hc}{E}$

Substitute the values:

$λ=\frac{6.6\times 10^{-34}\times 3.0\times 10^{8}}{3.96\times 10^{-19}}$

$λ=\frac{19.8\times 10^{-26}}{3.96\times 10^{-19}}$

$λ=5\times 10^{-7}\text{m}$

Convert into nm:

$1\text{m}=10^{9}\text{nm}$

$λ=5\times 10^{-7}\times 10^{9}$

$λ=5\times 10^{2}\text{nm}$

So,

$x=5$

Therefore, the required nearest integer is

$5$
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2026 (Online) 2nd April Evening Shift

text:
Consider the following gas phase reaction being carried out in a closed vessel at $25^{\circ }$C.
$2A(g)⟶4B(g)+C(g)$
time
(min)total pressure of the
system
(mm Hg)30300∞600The pressure of C(g) at 30 minutes time interval would be $________ mm Hg. ($nearest integer)
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 2nd April Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
For the reaction

$2A(g)⟶4B(g)+C(g)$

let the initial pressure of $A$ be $P_{0}$.

Since the vessel is closed and temperature is constant, pressure is proportional to number of moles.

At $t=\infty$, reaction is complete.

From the stoichiometry:

$2$ moles of $A$ produce $4+1=5$ moles of products

So if initially only $A$ is present, total moles increase by a factor

$\frac{5}{2}$

Hence final total pressure is

$P_{\infty }=\frac{5}{2}P_{0}$

Given:

$P_{\infty }=600\text{mm Hg}$

So,

$\frac{5}{2}P_{0}=600$

$P_{0}=600\times \frac{2}{5}=240\text{mm Hg}$

Now at $30$ min, let the extent of reaction correspond to consumption of $x$ pressure units of $A$ according to:

$2A\to 4B+C$

Then pressure changes are:

$A$: decreases by $x$

$B$: increases by $2x$

$C$: increases by $\frac{x}{2}$

This is because for $2A\to 4B+C$,

if $2$ units of $A$ react, $4$ units of $B$ and $1$ unit of $C$ are formed.

So total pressure at time $t$ is

$P_{t}=(240-x)+2x+\frac{x}{2}$

$P_{t}=240+\frac{3x}{2}$

Given at $30$ min,

$240+\frac{3x}{2}=300$

$\frac{3x}{2}=60$

$x=40$

Therefore pressure of $C$ at $30$ min is

$P_{C}=\frac{x}{2}=20\text{mm Hg}$

So, the required pressure is

$20\text{mm Hg}$
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2026 (Online) 2nd April Evening Shift

text:
Consider the following two half-cell reactions along with the standard reduction potential given :

$\mathrm{CO}_{2}+6\mathrm{H}^{+}+6e^{-}⟶\mathrm{CH}_{3}\mathrm{OH}+\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O}E_{\text{red}}^{\circ }=0.02\mathrm{V}$

$\dfrac{1}{2}\mathrm{O}_{2}+2\mathrm{H}^{+}+2e^{-}⟶\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O}E_{\text{red}}^{\circ }=1.23\mathrm{V}$

A fuel cell was set up using the above two reactions such that the cell operates under the standard condition of 1 bar pressure and 298 K temperature. The fuel cell works with 80% efficiency. If the work derived from the cell using 1 mol of $\mathrm{CH}_{3}\mathrm{OH}$ is used to compress an ideal gas isothermally against a constant pressure of 1 kPa, then the change in the volume of the gas,

$\Delta V=–$ m${}^{3}$. (nearest integer)

Given : $\mathrm{F}=96500\mathrm{C}\mathrm{mol}^{-1}$
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 2nd April Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
For the fuel cell, methanol will be oxidised and oxygen will be reduced.

Given reduction half-cells:

$\mathrm{CO}_{2}+6\mathrm{H}^{+}+6e^{-}⟶\mathrm{CH}_{3}\mathrm{OH}+\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O}E_{\text{red}}^{\circ }=0.02\mathrm{V}$

$\frac{1}{2}\mathrm{O}_{2}+2\mathrm{H}^{+}+2e^{-}⟶\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O}E_{\text{red}}^{\circ }=1.23\mathrm{V}$

Since methanol is the fuel, it will undergo oxidation. So we reverse the first reaction:

$\mathrm{CH}_{3}\mathrm{OH}+\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O}⟶\mathrm{CO}_{2}+6\mathrm{H}^{+}+6e^{-}$

Its oxidation potential is:

$E_{\text{ox}}^{\circ }=-0.02\mathrm{V}$

Now calculate standard cell potential:

$E_{\text{cell}}^{\circ }=E_{\text{cathode}}^{\circ }+E_{\text{anode(ox)}}^{\circ }$

$E_{\text{cell}}^{\circ }=1.23+(-0.02)=1.21\mathrm{V}$

Number of electrons transferred:

$n=6$

So maximum electrical work from 1 mol of $\mathrm{CH}_{3}\mathrm{OH}$ is

$w_{\max }=nFE_{\text{cell}}^{\circ }$

$w_{\max }=6\times 96500\times 1.21$

$w_{\max }=700590\mathrm{J}$

Fuel cell works with $80%$ efficiency, so actual work obtained is

$w=0.8\times 700590$

$w=560472\mathrm{J}$

This work is used to compress an ideal gas isothermally against constant pressure $P=1\text{kPa}=1000\text{Pa}$.

For compression against constant external pressure,

$w=P\Delta V$

So,

$\Delta V=\frac{w}{P}$

$\Delta V=\frac{560472}{1000}=560.472\mathrm{m}^{3}$

Nearest integer:

$\Delta V\approx 560\mathrm{m}^{3}$

Since it is compression, volume decreases. So strictly,

$\Delta V=-560\mathrm{m}^{3}$

If only magnitude is asked, then

$560$
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2026 (Online) 2nd April Evening Shift

text:
Number of paramagnetic ions among the following d- and f-block metal ions is $__________$.
$Mn^{2+}, Cu^{2+}, Zn^{2+}, Yb^{2+}, Sc^{3+}, La^{3+}, Gd^{3+}, Lu^{3+}, Ti^{4+}, Ce^{4+}$
(Atomic number of Mn = 25, Cu = 29, Zn = 30, Yb = 70, Sc = 21, La = 57, Gd = 64, Lu = 71, Ti = 22, Ce = 58)
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 2nd April Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
To find the number of paramagnetic ions, we check whether each ion has one or more unpaired electrons.

If all electrons are paired, the ion is diamagnetic.

We will write the electronic configuration of each ion.

1. $Mn^{2+}$
Atomic number of Mn $=25$

Neutral Mn:

$[Ar]3d^{5}4s^{2}$

For $Mn^{2+}$, remove two electrons from $4s$:

$Mn^{2+}=[Ar]3d^{5}$

There are $5$ unpaired electrons, so it is paramagnetic.

2. $Cu^{2+}$
Atomic number of Cu $=29$

Neutral Cu:

$[Ar]3d^{10}4s^{1}$

For $Cu^{2+}$, remove one electron from $4s$ and one from $3d$:

$Cu^{2+}=[Ar]3d^{9}$

There is $1$ unpaired electron, so it is paramagnetic.

3. $Zn^{2+}$
Atomic number of Zn $=30$

Neutral Zn:

$[Ar]3d^{10}4s^{2}$

For $Zn^{2+}$:

$Zn^{2+}=[Ar]3d^{10}$

All electrons are paired, so it is diamagnetic.

4. $Yb^{2+}$
Atomic number of Yb $=70$

Neutral Yb:

$[Xe]4f^{14}6s^{2}$

For $Yb^{2+}$:

$Yb^{2+}=[Xe]4f^{14}$

All electrons are paired, so it is diamagnetic.

5. $Sc^{3+}$
Atomic number of Sc $=21$

Neutral Sc:

$[Ar]3d^{1}4s^{2}$

For $Sc^{3+}$:

$Sc^{3+}=[Ar]$

No unpaired electron, so it is diamagnetic.

6. $La^{3+}$
Atomic number of La $=57$

Neutral La:

$[Xe]5d^{1}6s^{2}$

For $La^{3+}$:

$La^{3+}=[Xe]$

No unpaired electron, so it is diamagnetic.

7. $Gd^{3+}$
Atomic number of Gd $=64$

Neutral Gd:

$[Xe]4f^{7}5d^{1}6s^{2}$

For $Gd^{3+}$, remove $6s^{2}$ and $5d^{1}$:

$Gd^{3+}=[Xe]4f^{7}$

This has $7$ unpaired electrons, so it is paramagnetic.

8. $Lu^{3+}$
Atomic number of Lu $=71$

Neutral Lu:

$[Xe]4f^{14}5d^{1}6s^{2}$

For $Lu^{3+}$:

$Lu^{3+}=[Xe]4f^{14}$

All electrons are paired, so it is diamagnetic.

9. $Ti^{4+}$
Atomic number of Ti $=22$

Neutral Ti:

$[Ar]3d^{2}4s^{2}$

For $Ti^{4+}$:

$Ti^{4+}=[Ar]$

No unpaired electron, so it is diamagnetic.

10. $Ce^{4+}$
Atomic number of Ce $=58$

Neutral Ce:

$[Xe]4f^{1}5d^{1}6s^{2}$

For $Ce^{4+}$, remove four electrons:

$Ce^{4+}=[Xe]$

No unpaired electron, so it is diamagnetic.

Paramagnetic ions are:
$Mn^{2+},Cu^{2+},Gd^{3+}$

So, the number of paramagnetic ions is

$3$
